## Definitions and examples

This page demonstrates each environment, cross-references, display math, and
collapsible proofs and solutions. Remarks always stay visible.

::: {#def-even}
An integer $n$ is **even** if $n = 2k$ for some integer $k$.
:::

::: {#exm-even}
# An even square
Since $6 = 2 \cdot 3$, the integer $6$ is even, and so is $6^2 = 36$.
:::

::: {.remark}
The definition (@def-even) includes zero and negative integers.
:::

## Statements and proofs

::: {#lem-even-square}
The square of an even integer is even.
:::

::: {.proof key=even-square}
Write $n = 2k$ with $k$ an integer. Then $n^2 = 4k^2 = 2(2k^2)$ is even.
:::

::: {#cor-even-fourth}
If $n$ is even, then $n^4$ is even.
:::

::: {.proof key=even-fourth}
Apply @lem-even-square first to $n$, then to the even integer $n^2$.
:::

::: {#prp-asympt-inv}
# An asymptotic inverse
Let $a,c > 0$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}$. The function
$f(x) = cx^a(\ln x)^b$ has an inverse on a sufficiently far-out interval
$(x_0,\infty)$. As $y \to \infty$, this inverse satisfies
$$
f^{-1}(y) \sim a^{b/a}c^{-1/a}y^{1/a}(\ln y)^{-b/a}.
$$
:::

::: {.proof key=asymptotic-inverse}
Since
$$
f'(x) = cx^{a-1}(\ln x)^b\left(a + \frac{b}{\ln x}\right) > 0
$$
for all sufficiently large $x$, the function $f$ is eventually strictly
increasing. Also $\ln f(x) = \ln c + a\ln x + b\ln\ln x \to \infty$,
so $f(x) \to \infty$ and the stated inverse exists for large $y$.
Writing $x=f^{-1}(y)$ gives $x \to \infty$ and
$\ln y \sim a\ln x$. Consequently,
$$
x = c^{-1/a}y^{1/a}(\ln x)^{-b/a}
  \sim a^{b/a}c^{-1/a}y^{1/a}(\ln y)^{-b/a}.
$$
:::

::: {#thm-sum}
# Sum of the first integers
For every integer $n \ge 1$,
$$
\sum_{k=1}^n k = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}.
$$
:::

::: {.proof .expanded key=sum-of-integers}
The identity holds for $n=1$. If it holds for $n$, then
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{n+1} k = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} + (n+1)
= \frac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2},
$$
which proves the induction step.
:::

::: {#cnj-goldbach}
# Goldbach's conjecture
Every even integer greater than $2$ is the sum of two primes.
:::

## Exercise and solution

::: {#exr-odd-square}
Show that the square of an odd integer is odd.
:::

::: {#sol-odd-square}
1. Write the odd integer as $n=2k+1$ for an integer $k$.
2. Expand: $n^2=4k^2+4k+1=2(2k^2+2k)+1$, which is odd.
:::
